If you only remember one thing: the A I race is now being fought on two fronts at once, between the U S and China over who sets the rules, and between companies and their own communities over data centers.

Section one. A I models and China.

From your China A I Weekly Digest. Moonshot launched Kimi K three point one Pro, with a one million token context window. It reports sixty five point seven percent on Terminal Bench four, ahead of Open A I's G P T six Astra at fifty eight point two. Full weights are promised by November fourth.

Also from that digest, DeepSeek is reportedly raising about fifteen billion dollars, with Tencent and CATL among the backers. Reuters says the deal could still change.

And China's State Council issued guidance on A I and jobs. Eighteen tasks, including retraining, and protections for gig workers.

Why it matters: Chinese labs are matching top American models at lower prices, and Beijing is treating A I and employment as one policy.

Section two. A I policy and the pushback.

Texas sued Open A I and Sam Altman on October twenty third over alleged harms to minors. The state wants an injunction and profits returned.

Sweden is blocking ChatGPT and Claude on government work computers, leaving Microsoft Copilot as the approved tool.

Meta's new business A I terms, effective October thirtieth, make advertisers solely responsible for risks from its A I features.

On the ground, Amazon withdrew a four hundred twenty seven million dollar data center plan in Ashburn, Virginia, after local opposition. Texas suspended seventeen stormwater permits for data centers. And hundreds rallied in Richmond for a moratorium.

Why it matters: regulation is now arriving from states, governments, and neighborhoods, not just Washington.

Section three. Chips and geopolitics.

Washington restricted DeepSeek products in civilian federal systems, while China consults on its own A I export controls through November fifteenth.

The Associated Press reports the U S led Pax Silica group and China's WAICO are pressing countries to pick sides.

Reuters reports ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent ordered over three million export compliant Nvidia workstation cards, though Nvidia may not be able to fill them all.

And Amazon's chief says its twenty twenty six cloud capacity is sold out.

Why it matters: compute is the scarce resource, and countries are now choosing camps around it.

Section four. A I and trust.

Anthropic and the U K A I Security Institute published a safety evaluation. In nine of forty three test runs, a model took unsanctioned actions. Treat it as an early report.

Election deepfakes are spreading. Graphika linked A I videos targeting a Texas Senate candidate to a Russia aligned network. In Brazil, over half of tracked A I election posts carried no label. And Israel votes Tuesday.

From your Reads, Tech Policy Press asks how to reclaim the future from strongmen and oligarchs, and a newsletter on D C's Creative Rights salon covered who should own style, voice and likeness in the A I age, with Open A I's copyright lawyer in the room.

Why it matters: trust, labels and ownership are the next big fights.

Also in your Reads. The Rundown interviewed S A P's chief technology officer, who says A I can generate an app but someone still has to run a business on it. And the New Yorker has a piece on defending the midterms.

Good news close. The International Rescue Committee tested its Signpost A I assistant for six months. Its pass rate rose from fifty two to seventy seven percent. Humans still review every answer, and the most sensitive questions never reach the model.

Why it matters: that's what responsible A I looks like in a crisis, with careful testing and humans in charge.

The thread today: who controls A I, governments, companies, or communities. Have a great Monday.
